Central Nervous System
Anatomy
Spinal Cord

The spinal cord is the lower, cylindrical part of the central nervous system, extending from the foramen magnum to the level of the L1–L2 intervertebral disc in adults. It carries 31 pairs of spinal nerves, is protected by three meningeal layers, and receives a dedicated arterial and venous supply that keeps it independent from — but connected to — the cranial circulation.

This lesson covers its external features, internal grey/white matter organisation, spinal nerve roots and their course, the spinal meninges and CSF-related spaces, and the arterial and venous supply of the cord — all essential for understanding cord-level lesions, lumbar puncture, and spinal cord ischaemia.

External Features

The spinal cord is the long (average length 45 cm) lower cylindrical part of the CNS, occupying the upper two-thirds of the vertebral canal.

  • Beginning: At the foramen magnum, as a continuation of the medulla oblongata.
  • Termination:
    • Adults: opposite the intervertebral disc between L1 and L2.
    • Newborn: lower end reaches the level of L3; the adult level is not reached until 20 years of age.
  • Its lower end tapers into a cone called the conus medullaris.
  • Spinal enlargements: cervical and lumbar enlargements.

Fissures and Sulci

  • Anterior median fissure: a deep midline groove along the entire anterior aspect of the cord.
  • Posterior median sulcus: a shallow sulcus on the posterior aspect.
  • 2 anterolateral sulci & 2 posterolateral sulci: at the attachment of the spinal nerve roots.

A posterior median septum extends from the posterior median sulcus into the substance of the cord to a variable extent.

Spinal Cord Segments and Enlargements

A spinal segment is the portion of spinal cord that gives origin to a pair of spinal nerves. The cord has 31 spinal segments: 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, and 1 coccygeal. Segment size depends on the amount of tissue supplied by that segment.

EnlargementSpinal segmentsNerves formed
Cervical enlargementC5–T1Brachial plexus
Lumbar enlargementL2–S3Lumbar & sacral plexus

Internal Structure

A transverse section of the spinal cord reveals grey matter centrally and white matter peripherally.

Grey Matter

  • Central mass of grey matter: H-shaped; divided into symmetrical right and left masses connected across the midline by a transverse grey commissure.
  • Central canal: passes through the centre of the grey commissure.
  • Horns: each lateral mass of grey matter is divided into:
    • Posterior horn — sensory
    • Anterior horn — motor
    • Lateral horn — autonomic; present only in the thoracic segments and the upper two lumbar segments (T1–L2)

White Matter

In each half of the cord, the white matter is divided into three columns:

  • Posterior column — between the posterior median septum and the posterior horn.
  • Lateral column — between the anterior and posterior horns.
  • Anterior column — between the anterior median fissure and the anterior horn.

The anterior white columns of the two sides are joined together by the white commissure.

Spinal Nerves

31 pairs of spinal nerves emerge from the corresponding segments: 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, and 1 coccygeal. Each spinal nerve emerges by two roots:

  • Anterior root (motor root): emerges along the anterolateral sulcus.
  • Posterior root (sensory root): attached to the posterolateral sulcus.

The anterior and posterior roots unite within their appropriate intervertebral foramina to form the nerve trunk.

Direction and Exit of Spinal Nerve Roots

Because the spinal cord is shorter than the vertebral canal, the course of the spinal nerve roots to reach their intervertebral foramen varies with level. In addition, the number of nerves does not correspond to the number of vertebrae — there are 8 cervical nerves but only 7 cervical vertebrae — so the level of exit relative to the corresponding vertebra also varies.

Cauda Equina

The cauda equina is a bunch of lumbar (except L1), sacral, and coccygeal nerve roots surrounding the filum terminale within the pool of CSF (cauda = tail, equina = horse).

Spinal Meninges

Spinal Dura Mater

  • Outer, tough, dense layer, continuous with the cranial dura mater.
  • Extension: down to the lower border of the S2 vertebra.
  • Attachment: firmly attached to the foramen magnum, and to the tectorial membrane & posterior longitudinal ligament on the body of the axis vertebra.

Subdural and Epidural Spaces

  • Subdural space: between the spinal dura and arachnoid mater; contains a thin film of serous fluid.
  • Epidural space: between the spinal dura and the vertebrae; contains the internal vertebral venous plexus.

Spinal Arachnoid Mater

  • A thin, transparent, vascular membrane.
  • Extension: to the lower border of the S2 vertebra.

Subarachnoid Space

  • The space between the arachnoid mater and the pia mater.
  • Filled with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF).
  • Lumbar cistern: the widened subarachnoid space below the conus medullaris; it contains the cauda equina and filum terminale in a pool of CSF.
Clinical Correlation — Lumbar Puncture

A needle is introduced into the lumbar cistern between L3–L4 or L4–L5 vertebrae to withdraw CSF, or to inject anaesthetic agents or dye.

Spinal Pia Mater

A vascular membrane that closely invests the spinal cord. Its processes include:

  • Filum terminale:
    • Thin, thread-like prolongation of the pia mater beyond the conus medullaris.
    • Pierces the dura, passes through the sacral canal and hiatus.
    • Attachment: to the dorsum of the first coccyx piece.
  • Denticulate ligament:
    • 21 tooth-like lateral projections from the spinal pia.
    • Located between the dorsal and ventral nerve roots.
    • Pass through the subarachnoid space and arachnoid mater.
    • Attachment: to the inner surface of the dura.
Factors Fixing the Spinal Cord
  • Denticulate ligament
  • Filum terminale
  • Dura, by its attachment to the foramen magnum and posterior longitudinal ligament

Blood Supply of the Spinal Cord

Arterial Supply

1. Anterior Spinal Artery

  • Origin: from the vertebral arteries; each vertebral artery gives one small spinal branch, and the two unite to form a single anterior spinal artery.
  • Course: runs caudally in the anterior median fissure of the spinal cord.
  • Supply: the anterior two-thirds of the cord.

2. Posterior Spinal Arteries

  • Origin: vertebral artery or posterior inferior cerebellar artery.
  • Course: each artery runs down in the posterolateral sulcus.
  • Supply: the posterior one-third of the cord.

3. Spinal Branches of Segmental Arteries

  • Origin:
    • Neck: deep cervical, ascending cervical.
    • Thorax: posterior intercostal.
    • Abdomen: lumbar.
    • Pelvis: lateral sacral arteries.
  • Course: reach the cord as anterior and posterior radicular arteries along the corresponding nerve roots.
  • Supply: mainly nourish the nerve roots, and give medullary feeders to reinforce the spinal arteries.
Arteria Radicularis Magna

A large radicular artery arising from the lower posterior intercostal or upper lumbar arteries. It is the main source of supply to the lower part of the spinal cord. Its occlusion leads to lumbosacral cord ischaemia.

Venous Drainage

The veins draining the cord form six longitudinal venous channels around the cord:

  • Two median longitudinal veins — one in the anterior median fissure, one in the posteromedian sulcus.
  • Two anterolateral veins — one on each side, posterior to the anterior nerve roots.
  • Two posterolateral veins — one on each side, posterior to the posterior nerve roots.
  • Communication:
    • Superiorly: with the cranial dural venous sinuses.
    • In the vertebral canal: with the internal vertebral venous plexus.
  • Drainage: by radicular veins into segmental veins.
Clinical Note

The internal vertebral venous plexus is valveless and communicates with the cranial dural sinuses and the prostatic venous plexus below — so prostatic carcinoma can spread to the brain and meninges.

Key Points

Basic Dimensions

  • Average length: 45 cm
  • Begins at foramen magnum
  • Ends at L1–L2 disc (adult); L3 in newborn
  • Adult termination level reached by age 20

31 Segments

  • 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, 1 coccygeal
  • Cervical enlargement: C5–T1 → brachial plexus
  • Lumbar enlargement: L2–S3 → lumbosacral plexus

Grey Matter Horns

  • Posterior horn — sensory
  • Anterior horn — motor
  • Lateral horn — autonomic (T1–L2 only)

Nerve Roots

  • Anterior root = motor, from anterolateral sulcus
  • Posterior root = sensory, from posterolateral sulcus
  • Cauda equina = lumbar (except L1), sacral, coccygeal roots + filum terminale

Meninges & Spaces

  • Dura & arachnoid extend to lower border of S2
  • Epidural space: dura ↔ vertebrae (contains venous plexus)
  • Subarachnoid space: contains CSF; lumbar cistern below conus medullaris
  • Lumbar puncture: L3–L4 or L4–L5

Fixation of the Cord

  • Denticulate ligament
  • Filum terminale
  • Dural attachments (foramen magnum, posterior longitudinal ligament)

Arterial Supply

  • Anterior spinal artery → anterior 2/3 of cord
  • Posterior spinal arteries → posterior 1/3 of cord
  • Segmental radicular arteries nourish nerve roots
  • Arteria radicularis magna supplies lower cord; occlusion → lumbosacral ischaemia

Venous Drainage

  • 6 longitudinal channels (2 median, 2 anterolateral, 2 posterolateral)
  • Drains via radicular veins into segmental veins
  • Valveless plexus links to prostatic plexus → route for cancer spread
